subject: math
title: Grade 8 Views and Nets of 3D Objects
seo_title: Grade 8 Views and Nets Worksheets: Top, Front and Side Views, Nets of Prisms and Cylinders (Free, Answer Key, BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Construction, views, and nets of 3D objects
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 math worksheets on views and nets for the BC curriculum: top, front and side views of cube structures, matching objects to their views and mat plans, nets of prisms, pyramids and cylinders, and counting cubes from views. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: A view shows an object from one direction; a net is the flat pattern that folds into it.
key_sub: Front view: the tallest stack in each column. Right side view: the front of the object is on the left. Top view: one square per stack, front at the bottom. A cylinder’s net is a rectangle 2 × π × r long with a circle on each long edge.
body_html:
Top, front and side views

A view is what you see when you look straight at an object from one side. Each cube face you see becomes one square.

  • Front view: look from the front. Draw the tallest stack in each column, left to right.
  • Right side view: look from the right. The front of the object is on your left.
  • Top view: look down from above. Each stack is one square, and the front is at the bottom.
Example 1

How many cubes are in the structure above?

Count stack by stack, including hidden cubes: 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1.

Answer: 10 cubes

Mat plans

A mat plan is a top view with a number in each square: the number of cubes in that stack. Add the numbers to count the cubes. The largest number in each column gives the front view.

Three views do not always fix the number of cubes. Find the greatest number by making each stack as tall as both its column (front view) and its row (side view) allow.

Nets of prisms, pyramids and cylinders

A net is a flat pattern that folds into a 3D object. A prism has 2 matching bases joined by rectangles, one rectangle for each side of the base. A pyramid has 1 base and a triangle on each side. A cylinder has 2 circles and a rectangle.

The rectangle in a cylinder’s net wraps once around each circle, so its length is the circumference: 2 × π × r.

Example 2

A cylinder has a radius of 4 cm and a height of 10 cm. What are the dimensions of the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)

Length = 2 × 3.14 × 4 = 25.12 cm. The width is the height of the cylinder.

Answer: 25.12 cm by 10 cm

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Mixing up the front view and the side viewFind the red arrow (the front) first. The side view is seen from the right
Drawing the right side view backwardsFrom the right, the front of the object is on your left
Drawing a cube for every cube in the front viewDraw only the tallest stack in each column; cubes behind are hidden
Counting only the cubes you can seeCount each stack from the bottom, including hidden cubes
Putting both bases of a prism on the same edge of the netPut one base on each long edge of the strip of rectangles
Making a cylinder’s rectangle as long as the diameterIts length is the circumference: 2 × π × r

faq.q: What are top, front and side views in Grade 8 math?
faq.a: They are 2D drawings of a 3D object seen from straight above, straight in front and from the right side. Each view shows every cube face you can see from that direction as one square.

faq.q: Are views and nets in the BC Grade 8 math curriculum?
faq.a: Yes. “Construction, views, and nets of 3D objects” is a Grade 8 content standard in Geometry and measurement in the BC Mathematics Curriculum.

faq.q: What does the net of a cylinder look like?
faq.a: It is a rectangle with a circle on each of two opposite edges. The rectangle’s length is the circle’s circumference (2 × π × r) and its width is the height of the cylinder.

faq.q: How do you count the cubes from a mat plan?
faq.a: A mat plan is a top view with the number of cubes in each stack written in its square. Add all the numbers to get the total number of cubes.

items.q: A triangular prism is 10 cm long. Its bases are right triangles with sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. What is the size of the largest rectangle in its net?
items.e: Each rectangle is as wide as one side of the triangle and as long as the prism. The longest side is 10 cm, so the largest rectangle is 10 cm by 10 cm.

items.q: Which pattern is a net of a cube?
items.e: C folds into a cube with no gaps and no overlaps. Each of the others has two squares that fold onto the same face, so one face is left open.

items.q: What object can be made from this net?
items.e: 1 pentagon base and 5 triangles that meet at one point fold into a pentagonal pyramid.

items.q: This net is folded up. Which object does it make?
items.e: 1 square base and 4 triangles that meet at one point fold into a square-based pyramid.

items.q: Which net folds into a pentagonal prism?
items.e: B has 2 pentagons on opposite edges of a strip of 5 rectangles. One wrong net is a pentagonal pyramid, one has only 4 rectangles (it cannot close), and one has both pentagons on the same edge, so they fold onto the same end.

items.q: What object can be made from this net?
items.e: 2 triangles (the bases) and 3 rectangles fold into a triangular prism. The bases are right triangles here; a prism’s bases do not have to be equilateral.

items.q: Which net folds into a hexagonal prism?
items.e: D has 2 hexagons and 6 rectangles. One wrong net has only 5 rectangles, one is a hexagonal pyramid, and one has pentagons, so it makes a pentagonal prism.

items.q: Which 3D object does this net fold into?
items.e: 1 rectangle base and 4 triangles that meet at one point fold into a rectangular pyramid. The base is a rectangle that is not a square, so the triangles on the long sides and short sides differ.

items.q: This net is folded up. Which object does it make?
items.e: 1 hexagon base and 6 triangles that meet at one point fold into a hexagonal pyramid. A pyramid is named after its base.

items.q: How many faces does the net of a hexagonal prism have?
items.e: 2 hexagons (the bases) + 6 rectangles (one for each side of the hexagon) = 8 faces.

items.q: How many triangles are in the net of an octagonal pyramid?
items.e: An octagon has 8 sides, and there is one triangle on each side. The net has 8 triangles and 1 octagon (9 faces in all).

items.q: What object can be made from this net?
items.e: 2 pentagons (the bases) and 5 rectangles fold into a pentagonal prism.

items.q: Which net folds into a square-based pyramid?
items.e: A has 1 square and 4 triangles, one on each side of the square. One wrong net has only 3 triangles, so one side stays open. The others make a triangular prism and a triangular pyramid.

items.q: A net has 2 octagons and some rectangles. How many rectangles does it need to fold into a prism?
items.e: A prism has one rectangle for each side of its base. An octagon has 8 sides, so the net needs 8 rectangles.

items.q: A box is a rectangular prism 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm tall. How many faces in its net measure 30 cm by 10 cm?
items.e: The front and the back are both 30 cm by 10 cm. Opposite faces of a rectangular prism match, so faces come in pairs.

items.q: A net has 1 hexagon and 6 triangles. Which object does it make?
items.e: 1 hexagon base and 6 triangles that meet at one point fold into a hexagonal pyramid.

items.q: Which 3D object does this net fold into?
items.e: 6 rectangles in 3 matching pairs fold into a rectangular prism. Opposite faces are the same size.

items.q: Which 3D object does this net fold into?
items.e: 4 triangles fold into a triangular pyramid: one is the base and the other 3 meet at a point.

items.q: This net is folded up. Which object does it make?
items.e: 2 hexagons (the bases) and 6 rectangles fold into a hexagonal prism.

items.q: This net is folded into a cube. Which face is opposite face A?
items.e: Fold the net one square at a time: face E lands opposite face A. Faces that touch A in the net are next to it on the cube, never opposite.

items.q: The circles in a cylinder’s net have a diameter of 5 cm. The rectangle is 12 cm by 15.7 cm. What are the radius and the height of the cylinder?
items.e: The radius is half the diameter: 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 cm. The 15.7 cm edge wraps around the circle (3.14 × 5 = 15.7), so the other edge, 12 cm, is the height.

items.q: The rectangle in a cylinder’s net is 43.96 cm long, and that edge wraps around the circles. What is the radius of each circle? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: Circumference = π × d, so d = 43.96 ÷ 3.14 = 14 cm. The radius is half of that: 7 cm.

items.q: Which net folds into a closed cylinder?
items.e: C is right: the rectangle is as long as the distance around each circle. In one wrong net the rectangle is only as long as the diameter, so it is far too short to wrap around the circles. The others are a triangular prism and a net with only 1 circle.
A has a rectangle with one circle on each long edge, so the circles close both ends of the tube. One wrong net has only 1 circle, one has both circles on the same edge, and one is the net of a cone.

items.q: This is the net of a cylinder with radius 4 cm and height 9 cm. How long is the rectangle? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3.14 × 4 = 25.12 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: A cylinder has a radius of 6 cm and a height of 15 cm. How long is the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3.14 × 6 = 37.68 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: Which 3D object does this net fold into?
items.e: The rectangle rolls into a tube (the curved surface) and the 2 circles close the ends: a cylinder.

items.q: This is the net of a tall, thin tube. Why do the circles touch the short edges of the rectangle?
c: The short edges are as long as the diameter
Circles always go on the short edges
The long edges are the bottom
The short edges are as long as the circumference
items.e: The circles always touch the edges that wrap around them, and those edges are as long as the circumference. For a tall, thin tube, the circumference is shorter than the height, so these are the short edges.

items.q: A cylinder has a radius of 5 cm and a height of 12 cm. How long is the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: A can has a diameter of 16 cm. Its paper label wraps around the can once with no overlap. How long is the label? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: Circumference = π × d = 3.14 × 16 = 50.24 cm. 2 × π × d uses the diameter as if it were the radius.

items.q: The rectangle in a cylinder’s net is 31.4 cm long, and that edge wraps around the circles. What is the radius of each circle? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: Circumference = π × d, so d = 31.4 ÷ 3.14 = 10 cm. The radius is half of that: 5 cm.

items.q: In the net of a cylinder, the length of the rectangle that touches the circles is equal to …
items.e: That edge wraps once around each circle, so it is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r.

items.q: Olivia makes a model of a rain barrel shaped like a cylinder. The circles in her net have a radius of 10 cm. How long must the rectangle be? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: The rectangle wraps around the circles: 2 × 3.14 × 10 = 62.8 cm. 314 is π × r², the area of a circle.

items.q: A cylinder has a radius of 5 cm and a height of 10 cm. What is the area of the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: The rectangle is 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 cm long and 10 cm tall: 31.4 × 10 = 314 cm². 785 is π × r² × h (the volume), and 157 uses πr instead of 2πr.

items.q: The rectangle in a cylinder’s net is 12 cm by 18.84 cm. Each circle has a radius of 3 cm. How tall is the cylinder?
items.e: The edge that wraps around the circle is 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84 cm long. The other edge, 12 cm, is the height.

items.q: A cylinder has a radius of 9 cm and a height of 20 cm. How long is the rectangle in its net? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3.14 × 9 = 56.52 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: This is the net of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. How long is the rectangle? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: The rectangle is as long as the circumference: 2 × π × r = 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84 cm. Do not use πr (half the circle) or the diameter in place of r.

items.q: Which part of a cylinder’s net becomes the curved surface?
items.e: The rectangle rolls up into a tube. The 2 circles are the flat top and bottom.

items.q: A can has a diameter of 10 cm. Its paper label wraps around the can once with no overlap. How long is the label? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: Circumference = π × d = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 cm. 2 × π × d uses the diameter as if it were the radius.

items.q: A can has a diameter of 12 cm. Its paper label wraps around the can once with no overlap. How long is the label? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
items.e: Circumference = π × d = 3.14 × 12 = 37.68 cm. 2 × π × d uses the diameter as if it were the radius.

sets.title: Count the cubes: views and word problems

items.q: How many cubes are in this structure? Every stack stands on the table.
items.e: Count stack by stack, including the cubes hidden underneath and behind: 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 13. Counting only the cubes you can see gives 9.

items.q: A sculpture in Victoria is made of 1 m cubes. These are its top, front and right side views. What is the least number of cubes it could have?
items.e: Each stack in the top view needs at least 1 cube, and each column and row must reach the height in the front and side views. The fewest that works is 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 10. The greatest is 14.

items.q: Nadia builds this structure from 1 cm cubes. What is its volume?
items.e: Each 1 cm cube has a volume of 1 cm³. There are 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9 cubes, so the volume is 9 cm³ (cubic units, not cm²).

items.q: These are the top, front and right side views of a structure of cubes. How many cubes are in the structure?
items.e: The top view shows 4 stacks. Use the front and side views to find each stack’s height: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5. Adding the squares in the front and side views (3 + 4) counts some cubes twice.

items.q: The mat plan shows how many cubes are in each stack. How many cubes are there in all?
items.e: Add the numbers on the mat plan: 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 11. 8 is only the number of stacks.

items.q: These are the top, front and right side views of a structure of cubes. How many cubes are in the structure?
items.e: The top view shows 8 stacks. Use the front and side views to find each stack’s height: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 10. Adding the squares in the front and side views (5 + 4) counts some cubes twice.

items.q: Jasleen has 25 linking cubes. She builds this structure. How many cubes does she have left?
items.e: The structure has 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 13 cubes (count the hidden ones too). 25 − 13 = 12.

items.q: How many cubes are in this structure? Every stack stands on the table.
items.e: Count stack by stack, including the cubes hidden underneath and behind: 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 13. Counting only the cubes you can see gives 12.

items.q: Shipping containers at the Port of Vancouver are stacked in a solid block. The front view is 5 containers wide and 3 high. The right side view is 4 containers wide and 3 high. The top view is a full 5 by 4 rectangle. How many containers are in the block?
items.e: The top view shows 5 × 4 = 20 stacks, and every stack is 3 high: 20 × 3 = 60. Adding the views (15 + 12) counts the outside only.

items.q: These are the top, front and right side views of a structure of cubes. What is the greatest number of cubes it could have?
items.e: Make each stack as tall as both the front view (its column) and the side view (its row) allow: 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 8. The least possible is 7, so the views alone do not fix the number of cubes.

items.q: Lucas draws the front view of this structure on grid paper, one square for each cube face. How many squares does he shade?
items.e: From the front, the tallest stacks are 2, 1 and 1 cubes, so the view has 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 squares. Cubes behind the front ones are hidden and do not add squares.

items.q: Ji-woo wants every stack in this mat plan to be 3 cubes tall, to make a solid rectangular prism. How many more cubes does she need?
items.e: A solid prism 3 by 2 by 3 has 3 × 2 × 3 = 18 cubes. Ji-woo already has 12: 18 − 12 = 6.

items.q: How many cubes are in this structure? Every stack stands on the table.
items.e: Count stack by stack, including the cubes hidden underneath and behind: 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 9. Counting only the cubes you can see gives 6.

items.q: Zara builds a model of a Surrey apartment block from this mat plan. Each cube is one apartment. A cube on top of another is one floor higher. How many apartments are on the ground floor?
items.e: Every stack has exactly 1 cube on the ground floor, so count the stacks (the squares in the mat plan): 6. 9 is the number of apartments in the whole model.

items.q: These are the top, front and right side views of a structure of cubes. What is the greatest number of cubes it could have?
items.e: Make each stack as tall as both the front view (its column) and the side view (its row) allow: 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 13. The least possible is 10, so the views alone do not fix the number of cubes.

items.q: The mat plan shows how many cubes are in each stack. How many cubes are there in all?
items.e: Add the numbers on the mat plan: 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8. 5 is only the number of stacks.

items.q: How many cubes are in this structure? Every stack stands on the table.
items.e: Count stack by stack, including the cubes hidden underneath and behind: 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 10. Counting only the cubes you can see gives 7.

items.q: These are the top, front and right side views of a structure of cubes. How many cubes are in the structure?
items.e: The top view shows 5 stacks. Use the front and side views to find each stack’s height: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6. Adding the squares in the front and side views (4 + 3) counts some cubes twice.

items.q: How many cubes are in this structure? Every stack stands on the table.
items.e: Count stack by stack, including the cubes hidden underneath and behind: 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9. Counting only the cubes you can see gives 7.

items.q: Arjun builds a structure for a Kelowna art fair. Its top view is a full 3 by 2 rectangle. The front view is 3 cubes wide and 2 tall, and the right side view is 2 cubes wide and 2 tall. What is the greatest number of cubes he could use?
items.e: Every stack can be 2 cubes tall: 6 stacks × 2 = 12. The least is 9 (only 3 stacks need to be 2 tall). 10 adds the squares in the front and side views.
